claim: Dysfunction of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (mETC) is a major cause of human mitochondrial diseases.
source: Dysfunction of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (mETC) is a major cause of human mitochondrial diseases.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that represents established knowledge in the field of mitochondrial biology and disease.

claim: OCIAD1 is an inner mitochondrial membrane protein.
source: We find that OCIAD1 is an inner mitochondrial membrane protein that forms a complex with supramolecular prohibitin assemblies.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including carbonate extraction, protease protection assays, and immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3.

claim: OCIAD1 forms a complex with supramolecular prohibitin assemblies.
source: We find that OCIAD1 is an inner mitochondrial membrane protein that forms a complex with supramolecular prohibitin assemblies.
evidence: This is supported by affinity enrichment mass spectrometry data and BN-PAGE analysis showing co-migration with prohibitin complexes (Figure 4).

claim: OCIAD1 is required for maintenance of normal steady-state levels of Complex III.
source: Our data indicate that OCIAD1 is required for maintenance of normal steady-state levels of Complex III and the proteolytic processing of the catalytic subunit cytochrome c1 (CYC1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BN-PAGE analysis showing reduced Complex III levels in OCIAD1 knockdown cells (Figure 2).

claim: OCIAD1 is required for the proteolytic processing of the catalytic subunit cytochrome c1 (CYC1).
source: Our data indicate that OCIAD1 is required for maintenance of normal steady-state levels of Complex III and the proteolytic processing of the catalytic subunit cytochrome c1 (CYC1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and mass spectrometry data showing accumulation of unprocessed CYC1 forms in OCIAD1 knockdown cells (Figures 5 and 6).

claim: In OCIAD1 depleted mitochondria, unprocessed CYC1 is hemylated and incorporated into Complex III.
source: In OCIAD1 depleted mitochondria, unprocessed CYC1 is hemylated and incorporated into Complex III.
evidence: This is demonstrated by heme detection assays and 2D-native/SDS-PAGE analysis showing hemylated higher molecular weight CYC1 species in Complex III (Figures 5 and 6).

claim: OCIAD1 acts as an adaptor within prohibitin assemblies to stabilize and/or chaperone CYC1.
source: We propose that OCIAD1 acts as an adaptor within prohibitin assemblies to stabilize and/or chaperone CYC1 and to facilitate its proteolytic processing by the IMMP2L protease.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings showing OCIAD1 interaction with prohibitins and its requirement for CYC1 processing.

claim: OCIAD1 facilitates proteolytic processing of CYC1 by the IMMP2L protease.
source: We propose that OCIAD1 acts as an adaptor within prohibitin assemblies to stabilize and/or chaperone CYC1 and to facilitate its proteolytic processing by the IMMP2L protease.
evidence: This is supported by the identification of IMMP2L in the OCIAD1 interactome and the accumulation of unprocessed CYC1 in OCIAD1 knockdown cells.

claim: Mitochondria produce most of the ATP in eukaryotic cells through oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS).
source: Mitochondria are double membrane-bound organelles of endosymbiotic origin that produce most of the ATP in eukaryotic cells through oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) (Mitchell, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology supported by a citation.

claim: OXPHOS depends on the mitochondrial electron transport chain (mETC).
source: OXPHOS depends on the mitochondrial electron transport chain (mETC), which transfers electrons from NADH and succinate to molecular oxygen.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of oxidative phosphorylation.

claim: The mETC is comprised of a series of four large inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) complexes (CI–CIV) that assemble into supercomplexes of defined stoichiometry.
source: The mETC is comprised of a series of four large inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) complexes (CI–CIV) that assemble into supercomplexes of defined stoichiometry (Letts and Sazanov, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mETC structure supported by a citation.

claim: Perturbing the assembly or function of the mETC can lead to multisystem mitochondrial disorders.
source: Perturbing the assembly or function of the mETC can lead to multisystem mitochondrial disorders (Chinnery, 1993; Rodenburg, 2016; Tucker et al., 2013; Wanschers et al., 2014) and is linked to more general pathologies, such as diabetes (Antoun et al., 2015; Ramírez-Camacho et al., 2020), neurodegeneration (Devi et al., 2008; Giachin et al., 2016; Keeney et al., 2006), heart diseases (Andreu et al., 2000; Casademont and Miró, 2002; Hagen et al., 2013; Valnot et al., 1999), and cancer (Hoekstra and Bayley, 2013; Janeway et al., 2011; Pantaleo et al., 2014; Urra et al., 2017; Van Vranken et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: mETC dysfunction is linked to diabetes.
source: Perturbing the assembly or function of the mETC can lead to multisystem mitochondrial disorders (Chinnery, 1993; Rodenburg, 2016; Tucker et al., 2013; Wanschers et al., 2014) and is linked to more general pathologies, such as diabetes (Antoun et al., 2015; Ramírez-Camacho et al., 2020), neurodegeneration (Devi et al., 2008; Giachin et al., 2016; Keeney et al., 2006), heart diseases (Andreu et al., 2000; Casademont and Miró, 2002; Hagen et al., 2013; Valnot et al., 1999), and cancer (Hoekstra and Bayley, 2013; Janeway et al., 2011; Pantaleo et al., 2014; Urra et al., 2017; Van Vranken et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: mETC dysfunction is linked to neurodegeneration.
source: Perturbing the assembly or function of the mETC can lead to multisystem mitochondrial disorders (Chinnery, 1993; Rodenburg, 2016; Tucker et al., 2013; Wanschers et al., 2014) and is linked to more general pathologies, such as diabetes (Antoun et al., 2015; Ramírez-Camacho et al., 2020), neurodegeneration (Devi et al., 2008; Giachin et al., 2016; Keeney et al., 2006), heart diseases (Andreu et al., 2000; Casademont and Miró, 2002; Hagen et al., 2013; Valnot et al., 1999), and cancer (Hoekstra and Bayley, 2013; Janeway et al., 2011; Pantaleo et al., 2014; Urra et al., 2017; Van Vranken et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: mETC dysfunction is linked to heart diseases.
source: Perturbing the assembly or function of the mETC can lead to multisystem mitochondrial disorders (Chinnery, 1993; Rodenburg, 2016; Tucker et al., 2013; Wanschers et al., 2014) and is linked to more general pathologies, such as diabetes (Antoun et al., 2015; Ramírez-Camacho et al., 2020), neurodegeneration (Devi et al., 2008; Giachin et al., 2016; Keeney et al., 2006), heart diseases (Andreu et al., 2000; Casademont and Miró, 2002; Hagen et al., 2013; Valnot et al., 1999), and cancer (Hoekstra and Bayley, 2013; Janeway et al., 2011; Pantaleo et al., 2014; Urra et al., 2017; Van Vranken et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: mETC dysfunction is linked to cancer.
source: Perturbing the assembly or function of the mETC can lead to multisystem mitochondrial disorders (Chinnery, 1993; Rodenburg, 2016; Tucker et al., 2013; Wanschers et al., 2014) and is linked to more general pathologies, such as diabetes (Antoun et al., 2015; Ramírez-Camacho et al., 2020), neurodegeneration (Devi et al., 2008; Giachin et al., 2016; Keeney et al., 2006), heart diseases (Andreu et al., 2000; Casademont and Miró, 2002; Hagen et al., 2013; Valnot et al., 1999), and cancer (Hoekstra and Bayley, 2013; Janeway et al., 2011; Pantaleo et al., 2014; Urra et al., 2017; Van Vranken et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Coordination of mETC subunits of dual origin occurs in part via the formation of modular intermediates within mitochondria that assemble sequentially into functional complexes.
source: Coordination of mETC subunits of dual origin occurs in part via the formation of modular intermediates within mitochondria that assemble sequentially into functional complexes (Aich et al., 2018; Guerrero-Castillo et al., 2017; Lobo-Jarne et al., 2020; Ndi et al., 2018; Stephan and Ott, 2020; Van Vranken et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Assembly of mETCs strategically occurs in specialized domains that link protein import, membrane insertion, and assembly machineries.
source: Assembly of mETCs strategically occurs in specialized domains that link protein import, membrane insertion, and assembly machineries (Singh et al., 2020; Stoldt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Prohibitins are thought to promote mETC assembly and quality control by assembling into inner membrane ring‐like scaffold structures that specify local protein and lipid composition.
source: Prohibitins are thought to promote mETC assembly and quality control by assembling into inner membrane ring‐like scaffold structures that specify local protein and lipid composition (Nijtmans et al., 2000; Singh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In mammalian cells, prohibitins associate with a variety of inner membrane proteins, including mitochondrial translocases, subunits of mETC, the DnaJ-like chaperone DNACJ19, and matrix-AAA (m-AAA) proteases.
source: In mammalian cells, prohibitins associate with a variety of inner membrane proteins, including mitochondrial translocases, subunits of mETC, the DnaJ-like chaperone DNACJ19, and matrix-AAA (m-AAA) proteases (Nijtmans et al., 2000; Richter-Dennerlein et al., 2014; Steglich et al., 1999; Yoshinaka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Complex III is an obligate homodimeric enzyme (CIII2) embedded in the inner membrane with each monomer composed of 10–11 subunits.
source: Complex III is an obligate homodimeric enzyme (CIII2) embedded in the inner membrane with each monomer composed of 10–11 subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Complex III structure.

claim: Only three subunits of Complex III contain catalytically active redox groups: cytochrome b (MT-CYB), cytochrome c1 (CYC1), and the Rieske iron–sulfur protein (UQCRFS1).
source: Only three subunits contain catalytically active redox groups: cytochrome b (MT-CYB), cytochrome c1 (CYC1), and the Rieske iron–sulfur protein (UQCRFS1), with other accessory subunits that likely stabilize the assembly (Lee et al., 2001; Malaney et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A genome-wide CRISPRi screen identified 217 genes that significantly modulated sensitivity to antimycin A under oxidative conditions.
source: Using this approach, we identified 217 genes that significantly modulated sensitivity to antimycin A under oxidative conditions (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the genome-wide CRISPRi screen.

claim: Knockdown of 128 genes protected against antimycin A.
source: Knockdown of 128 of these genes protected against antimycin A.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the genome-wide CRISPRi screen.

claim: Gene ontology enrichment analysis of genes that protected against antimycin A identified an enrichment of genes encoding for mitochondrial respiratory chain Complex I.
source: Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis performed on this group identified an enrichment of genes encoding for mitochondrial respiratory chain Complex I.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of the screen data.

claim: Complex I is composed of 44 unique subunits, 37 of which are encoded by the nuclear DNA with the remaining seven subunits encoded by the mitochondrial genome.
source: Complex I is the most upstream entry point into the electron transport chain and is composed of 44 unique subunits, 37 of which are encoded by the nuclear DNA with the remaining seven subunits encoded by the mitochondrial genome (Fiedorczuk et al., 2016; Guerrero-Castillo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Complex I composition supported by citations.

claim: Knockdown of about one-sixth of the nuclear-encoded Complex I subunits, as well as additional assembly factors, significantly protected against antimycin A treatment.
source: Knockdown of about one-sixth of the nuclear-encoded Complex I subunits, as well as additional assembly factors, significantly protected against antimycin A treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the genome-wide CRISPRi screen shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knockdown of genes encoding components of the TCA cycle protected against antimycin A treatment.
source: Knockdown of genes encoding components of the TCA cycle also protected against antimycin A treatment, including those encoding enzymes that participate in both forward flux through this pathway to maintain OXPHOS and reverse flux for reductive carboxylation.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the genome-wide CRISPRi screen.

claim: Knockdown of 89 genes sensitized cells to antimycin A treatment.
source: In our screen, knockdown of 89 genes sensitized cells to antimycin A treatment (Figure 1B), including 9 of the 15 nuclear-encoded Complex III subunits or assembly factors (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the genome-wide CRISPRi screen shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 9 of the 15 nuclear-encoded Complex III subunits or assembly factors sensitized cells to antimycin A treatment when knocked down.
source: In our screen, knockdown of 89 genes sensitized cells to antimycin A treatment (Figure 1B), including 9 of the 15 nuclear-encoded Complex III subunits or assembly factors (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the genome-wide CRISPRi screen shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: GO enrichment analysis identified Complex III as the most enriched term for antimycin A toxicity.
source: Consistent with this, GO enrichment analysis identified Complex III as the most enriched term for antimycin A toxicity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of the screen data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: OCIAD1 was identified as a strongly sensitizing hit in the antimycin A screen.
source: In addition to genes encoding Complex III, OCIAD1 was identified as a strongly sensitizing hit (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the genome-wide CRISPRi screen shown in Figure 1B.

claim: OCIAD1 encodes a poorly characterized predicted transmembrane protein.
source: OCIAD1 encodes a poorly characterized predicted transmembrane protein (Figure 3A) that is aberrantly expressed in ovarian carcinomas and implicated in the regulation of mitochondrial metabolism via Complex I (Shetty et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on prior knowledge and a citation, with the transmembrane prediction shown in Figure 3A.

claim: OCIAD1 is aberrantly expressed in ovarian carcinomas.
source: OCIAD1 encodes a poorly characterized predicted transmembrane protein (Figure 3A) that is aberrantly expressed in ovarian carcinomas and implicated in the regulation of mitochondrial metabolism via Complex I (Shetty et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: OCIAD1 has been implicated in the regulation of mitochondrial metabolism via Complex I.
source: OCIAD1 encodes a poorly characterized predicted transmembrane protein (Figure 3A) that is aberrantly expressed in ovarian carcinomas and implicated in the regulation of mitochondrial metabolism via Complex I (Shetty et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Silencing OCIAD1 selectively compromised growth of antimycin A-treated cells, but not growth of oligomycin-treated cells.
source: Silencing OCIAD1 selectively compromised growth of antimycin A-treated cells, but not growth of oligomycin-treated cells (Figure 1D), suggesting, together with our screen data, that OCIAD1 knockdown specifically sensitizes cells to inhibition of Complex III.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from growth competition assays shown in Figure 1D.

claim: OCIAD1 knockdown specifically sensitizes cells to inhibition of Complex III.
source: Silencing OCIAD1 selectively compromised growth of antimycin A-treated cells, but not growth of oligomycin-treated cells (Figure 1D), suggesting, together with our screen data, that OCIAD1 knockdown specifically sensitizes cells to inhibition of Complex III.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective sensitivity to antimycin A (Complex III inhibitor) but not oligomycin (ATP synthase inhibitor).

claim: There were no significant defects observed in the assembly of Complex I, II, IV, or V in OCIAD1 knockdown cells.
source: There were no significant defects observed in the assembly of Complex I, II, IV, or V (Figure 2B,C,E and F).
evidence: This is based on BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 2B, C, E, and F.

claim: A selective defect in Complex III assembly was observed in cells depleted of OCIAD1.
source: By contrast, we observed a selective defect in Complex III assembly in cells depleted of OCIAD1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The abundance of Complex III was significantly reduced in mitochondria from OCIAD1 knockdown cells.
source: The abundance of Complex III was significantly reduced in mitochondria from OCIAD1 knockdown cells and restored to wildtype levels by OCIAD1 reintroduction, indicating that this defect is specific to loss of OCIAD1 function (Figure 2D, CIII2).
evidence: This is based on BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Complex III abundance was restored to wildtype levels by OCIAD1 reintroduction.
source: The abundance of Complex III was significantly reduced in mitochondria from OCIAD1 knockdown cells and restored to wildtype levels by OCIAD1 reintroduction, indicating that this defect is specific to loss of OCIAD1 function (Figure 2D, CIII2).
evidence: This is based on BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The Complex III assembly defect is specific to loss of OCIAD1 function.
source: The abundance of Complex III was significantly reduced in mitochondria from OCIAD1 knockdown cells and restored to wildtype levels by OCIAD1 reintroduction, indicating that this defect is specific to loss of OCIAD1 function (Figure 2D, CIII2).
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment showing restoration of Complex III levels upon OCIAD1 reintroduction.

claim: A smaller but significant reduction in CIII2 supercomplex assemblies was observed in OCIAD1 knockdown cells.
source: We also observed a smaller but significant reduction in CIII2 supercomplex assemblies (Figure 2D, SC).
evidence: This is based on BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes proteins are unusually long-lived.
source: Mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes proteins are unusually long-lived (Fornasiero et al., 2018) and thus, the smaller impact of OCIAD1 on supercomplexes might be a consequence of enhanced stability of supercomplexes compared to individual complexes.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The smaller impact of OCIAD1 on supercomplexes might be a consequence of enhanced stability of supercomplexes compared to individual complexes.
source: Mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes proteins are unusually long-lived (Fornasiero et al., 2018) and thus, the smaller impact of OCIAD1 on supercomplexes might be a consequence of enhanced stability of supercomplexes compared to individual complexes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: OCIAD1 primarily localized to mitochondria in U2OS cells.
source: Consistent with the MitoCarta repository, we found that OCIAD1 primarily localized to mitochondria in U2OS cells, as evidenced by indirect immunofluorescence analysis using validated polyclonal OCIAD1 antibodies (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: OCIAD1 is an integral membrane protein.
source: Following extraction of peripheral membrane proteins with carbonate treatment of increasing pH, OCIAD1 and the known inner membrane protein TIM50 (Yamamoto et al., 2002) both remained in the membrane pellet fraction isolated by differential centrifugation (Figure 3C). In contrast, the peripheral membrane proteins ATP5A1 and SDHA were readily extracted and found in the supernatant (Figure 3C). These data indicate that OCIAD1 is an integral membrane protein, consistent with the presence of two predicted transmembrane domains (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on carbonate extraction assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: OCIAD1 has two predicted transmembrane domains.
source: These data indicate that OCIAD1 is an integral membrane protein, consistent with the presence of two predicted transmembrane domains (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic prediction shown in Figure 3A.

claim: OCIAD1 was resistant to proteinase K degradation when intact mitochondria were treated.
source: Whereas the validated OMM protein TOM70 was digested by treatment of intact mitochondria with proteinase K, OCIAD1 was resistant to degradation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on protease protection assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: OCIAD1 was susceptible to proteolytic degradation after compromising OMM integrity by hypo-osmotic treatment.
source: OCIAD1 was however susceptible to proteolytic degradation after compromising OMM integrity by hypo-osmotic treatment, similar to other IMM proteins (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on protease protection assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The C-terminus of OCIAD1 localized to the intermembrane space.
source: OCIAD1 proteolytic fragments were not observed by Western analysis of mitoplasts treated with proteinase K (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C). Thus, given the location of the OCIAD1 epitope, this observation suggests that the C-terminus was degraded and therefore localized to the intermembrane space (IMS).
evidence: This is inferred from protease protection assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: OCIAD1 is a transmembrane protein embedded in the mitochondrial inner membrane with its N- and C-termini facing the IMS.
source: With a validated topology assay in hand, we transiently expressed OCIAD1 tagged with GFP11 at either the N- or C-terminus and observed GFP signal only in the IMS-targeted GFP1–10 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). Together, these data indicate that OCIAD1 is a transmembrane protein embedded in the mitochondrial inner membrane with its N- and C-termini facing the IMS (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on split GFP complementation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and summarized in Figure 3E.

claim: Complex III subunits and assembly factors were identified as potential OCIAD1 interactors by affinity enrichment mass spectrometry.
source: We identified Complex III subunits and assembly factors, which supports our BN-PAGE data indicating that OCIAD1 regulates Complex III assembly (Figure 4A, in green).
evidence: This is based on affinity enrichment mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Subunits of the prohibitin complex, PHB1 and PHB2, were identified as potential OCIAD1 interactors.
source: In addition, we identified subunits of the prohibitin complex, PHB1 and PHB2, as potential OCIAD1 interactors (Figure 4A, in dark purple), consistent with previously published work (Richter-Dennerlein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on affinity enrichment mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A and supported by a citation.

claim: Several prohibitin interactors were identified in the OCIAD1 interactome, including C1QBP, COX4I1, DNAJC19, the mitochondrial m-AAA proteases AFG3L2 and SPG7, MAIP1, and the protease IMMP2L.
source: We also identified several prohibitin interactors, including C1QBP, COX4I1, and DNAJC19, the mitochondrial m-AAA proteases AFG3L2 and SPG7, as well as the AFG3L2-interactor MAIP1, and the protease IMMP2L, all previously identified in published studies examining the prohibitin interactome (Richter-Dennerlein et al., 2014; Yoshinaka et al., 2019; Figure 4A, in light green).
evidence: This is based on affinity enrichment mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A and supported by citations.

claim: Prohibitins form large hetero-oligomeric ring complexes composed of assemblies of PHB1/PHB2 dimers in the inner membrane of mitochondria.
source: Prohibitins form large hetero-oligomeric ring complexes composed of assemblies of PHB1/PHB2 dimers in the inner membrane of mitochondria (Tatsuta et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Prohibitin structures are thought to constitute molecular scaffolds that define functional domains to regulate the lateral distribution of membrane lipids and proteins within the IMM.
source: These complexes are thought to constitute molecular scaffolds that define functional domains to regulate the lateral distribution of membrane lipids and proteins within the IMM (Osman et al., 2009; Richter-Dennerlein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Prohibitins and the related SPFH scaffold, SLP2, have been shown to sequester inner membrane associated proteases to gate their access to proteolytic substrates.
source: Consistent with this model, prohibitins and the related SPFH scaffold, SLP2, have been shown to sequester inner membrane associated proteases to gate their access to proteolytic substrates (Merkwirth et al., 2008; Steglich et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The majority of OCIAD1 associates with large 0.9–1 MDa supramolecular assemblies that co-migrate with prohibitin.
source: This analysis demonstrated that the majority of OCIAD1 associates with large 0.9–1 MDa supramolecular assemblies that co-migrate with prohibitin (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is based on BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Pre-incubation of mitochondrial membranes with anti-PHB2 antibody retarded the migration of both PHB2 and OCIAD1 supramolecular assemblies to a similar degree.
source: Pre-incubation of mitochondrial membranes with anti-PHB2 antibody, but not vehicle, retarded the migration of both PHB2 and OCIAD1 supramolecular assemblies to a similar degree (Figure 4D, compare dashed and solid lane line scans, respectively).
evidence: This is based on in-gel mobility shift assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: OCIAD1 associates with prohibitin complexes in the IMM.
source: Thus, together our data indicate that OCIAD1 associates with prohibitin complexes in the IMM.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-migration and mobility shift assay data.

claim: OCIAD1 has a paralog in vertebrates, OCIAD2, which likely arose from tandem gene duplication of a common ancestor around 435–500 million years ago.
source: OCIAD1 has a paralog in vertebrates, OCIAD2, which likely arose from tandem gene duplication of a common ancestor around 435–500 million years ago (Sinha et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: OCIAD1 and OCIAD2 share domain structure and significant homology.
source: The paralogs share domain structure and significant homology (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and have been reported to hetero-oligomerize (Sinha et al., 2018), suggesting a shared function.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and supported by a citation.

claim: OCIAD1 and OCIAD2 have been reported to hetero-oligomerize.
source: The paralogs share domain structure and significant homology (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and have been reported to hetero-oligomerize (Sinha et al., 2018), suggesting a shared function.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: OCIAD2 localized to mitochondria with a topology similar to OCIAD1.
source: Using indirect immunofluorescence, carbonate extraction, and protease protection analysis, we showed that, as expected, OCIAD2 localized to mitochondria with a topology similar to OCIAD1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: OCIAD2 was not a hit in the antimycin A screen.
source: OCIAD2 was not a hit in our antimycin A screen (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) and Western blot analysis indicated that the K562 cells used in our CRISPRi screen do not express OCIAD2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on screen data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: K562 cells used in the CRISPRi screen do not express OCIAD2.
source: OCIAD2 was not a hit in our antimycin A screen (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) and Western blot analysis indicated that the K562 cells used in our CRISPRi screen do not express OCIAD2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Knockdown of OCIAD1 in U2OS cells decreased steady-state levels of CIII2 relative to control cells.
source: Knockdown of OCIAD1 in U2OS cells decreased steady-state levels of CIII2 relative to control cells, consistent with our observations in K562 cells.
evidence: This is based on BN-PAGE analysis of U2OS cells.

claim: Knockdown of OCIAD2 did not affect CIII2 levels.
source: In contrast, knockdown of OCIAD2 did not affect CIII2 levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is based on BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: CIII2 abundance was markedly reduced in mitochondria from OCIAD1 knockdown cells grown in glucose media, but not in OCIAD2 knockdown cells.
source: Similar to galactose media, CIII2 abundance was markedly reduced in mitochondria from OCIAD1 knockdown cells grown in glucose media, but not in OCIAD2 knockdown cells, indicating that OCIAD1, but not OCIAD2, affects the assembly of Complex III under our experimental conditions.
evidence: This is based on BN-PAGE analysis of cells grown in glucose media.

claim: OCIAD1, but not OCIAD2, affects the assembly of Complex III under the experimental conditions tested.
source: Similar to galactose media, CIII2 abundance was markedly reduced in mitochondria from OCIAD1 knockdown cells grown in glucose media, but not in OCIAD2 knockdown cells, indicating that OCIAD1, but not OCIAD2, affects the assembly of Complex III under our experimental conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of OCIAD1 and OCIAD2 knockdown on CIII2 levels.

claim: The proteome was resilient to loss of OCIAD1 and OCIAD2 expression, as only 40 proteins were significantly affected in at least one of the different cell lines.
source: Overall, the proteome was resilient to loss of OCIAD1 and OCIAD2 expression, as only 40 proteins were significantly affected in at least one of the different cell lines (Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on untargeted quantitative mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: Hierarchical clustering identified a small cluster tightly associated with OCIAD1, containing 4 of the 10 subunits of Complex III, including UQCRC1, UQCRC2, UQCRB, and CYC1, as well as COX7A2L.
source: Hierarchical clustering of significantly affected proteins identified a small cluster tightly associated with OCIAD1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A, red box), containing 4 of the 10 subunits of Complex III, including UQCRC1, UQCRC2, UQCRB, and CYC1, as well as COX7A2L, which regulates Complex III biogenesis by promoting the assembly of CIII2 with CIV to form the CIII2CIV supercomplex (Cogliati et al., 2016; Lapuente-Brun et al., 2013; Lobo-Jarne et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering analysis of proteomics data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A.

claim: COX7A2L regulates Complex III biogenesis by promoting the assembly of CIII2 with CIV to form the CIII2CIV supercomplex.
source: Hierarchical clustering of significantly affected proteins identified a small cluster tightly associated with OCIAD1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A, red box), containing 4 of the 10 subunits of Complex III, including UQCRC1, UQCRC2, UQCRB, and CYC1, as well as COX7A2L, which regulates Complex III biogenesis by promoting the assembly of CIII2 with CIV to form the CIII2CIV supercomplex (Cogliati et al., 2016; Lapuente-Brun et al., 2013; Lobo-Jarne et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: All proteins in the OCIAD1-associated cluster were selectively downregulated in the individual OCIAD1 knockdown and OCIAD1/OCIAD2 double knockdown cell lines, but unaffected in the OCIAD1 rescued cell line and in OCIAD2 knockdown cells.
source: All proteins in this cluster were selectively downregulated in the individual OCIAD1 knockdown and OCIAD1/OCIAD2 double knockdown cell lines, but unaffected in the OCIAD1 rescued cell line and in OCIAD2 knockdown cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is based on proteomics data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Steady-state levels of UQCRC1, UQCRC2, and CYC1 were reduced in mitochondria isolated from OCIAD1 knockdown cells, but not OCIAD2 knockdown cells.
source: We validated these observations using Western blotting and showed that steady-state levels of UQCRC1, UQCRC2, and CYC1 were reduced in mitochondria isolated from OCIAD1 knockdown cells, but not OCIAD2 knockdown cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B and Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B and Figure 5E,F.

claim: OCIAD2, like OCIAD1, co-migrates with prohibitin complexes independent of OCIAD1.
source: Although OCIAD2 does not have a measurable effect on Complex III biogenesis under our conditions, BN-PAGE analysis and Western analysis of mitochondria from U2OS cells using anti-OCIAD2 antibody demonstrated that, like OCIAD1, OCIAD2 co-migrates with prohibitin complexes independent of OCIAD1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: OCIAD2 is not required for the association of OCIAD1 with prohibitin complexes.
source: Reciprocally, OCIAD2 is not required for the association of OCIAD1 with prohibitin complexes as OCIAD1 migrated as 0.9–1 MDa assemblies in K562 cells that do not express OCIAD2 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is inferred from BN-PAGE analysis of K562 cells shown in Figure 4C.

claim: OCIAD1 and OCIAD2 paralogs experienced functional diversification during evolution.
source: Therefore, our data suggest that OCIAD1 and OCIAD2 paralogs experienced functional diversification during evolution.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of OCIAD1 and OCIAD2 on Complex III assembly.

claim: A highly conserved phenylalanine residue (F102) was identified within a segment of the conserved OCIA domain essential for OCIAD1 function in CIII2 assembly.
source: Sequence alignments of OCIAD1 genes from distant phylogenetic species identified a highly conserved phenylalanine residue (F102) within this region (Figure 4—figure supplement 5C, red box), which we mutated to an alanine.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5C.

claim: Cells expressing the OCIAD1 F102A mutant had decreased levels of Complex III.
source: In contrast to cells expressing wildtype OCIAD1, cells expressing the F102A mutant had decreased levels of Complex III, indicating that F102A constitutes a loss-of-function mutation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: F102A constitutes a loss-of-function mutation in OCIAD1.
source: In contrast to cells expressing wildtype OCIAD1, cells expressing the F102A mutant had decreased levels of Complex III, indicating that F102A constitutes a loss-of-function mutation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is inferred from the failure of the F102A mutant to rescue Complex III levels.

claim: CYC1 was selectively enriched in cells rescued with wildtype OCIAD1 versus OCIAD1 F102A.
source: This analysis revealed a selective enrichment of CYC1, one of three catalytic CIII2 subunits, in cells rescued with wildtype OCIAD1 versus OCIAD1 F102A Figure 5C (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on affinity enrichment mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The function of OCIAD1 in Complex III assembly is dependent on its interaction with CYC1.
source: These data suggest that the function of OCIAD1 in Complex III assembly is dependent on its interaction with CYC1.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective enrichment of CYC1 in wildtype OCIAD1 versus F102A mutant.

claim: CYC1 contains a single covalently attached heme prosthetic group that facilitates the transfer of electrons from the Rieske iron–sulfur protein to cytochrome c.
source: CYC1 contains a single covalently attached heme prosthetic group that facilitates the transfer of electrons from the Rieske iron–sulfur protein to cytochrome c.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CYC1 function.

claim: CYC1 is synthesized on cytosolic ribosomes as an apoenzyme precursor with a bipartite signal sequence that is processed in two steps during import.
source: It is synthesized on cytosolic ribosomes as an apoenzyme precursor with a bipartite signal sequence that is processed in two steps during import.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CYC1 biogenesis.

claim: The CYC1 precursor is first processed to an intermediate form by the matrix metalloprotease (MPP), which removes the matrix targeting sequence.
source: The CYC1 precursor is first processed to an intermediate form by the matrix metalloprotease (MPP), which removes the matrix targeting sequence (Gasser et al., 1982; Ndi et al., 2018; Nicholson et al., 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The stop transfer signal of CYC1 is processed by IMMP2L, a signal peptidase-like protease.
source: The stop transfer signal is processed by IMMP2L, a signal peptidase-like protease (Gasser et al., 1982; Ndi et al., 2018; Nicholson et al., 1989; Nunnari et al., 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: IMMP2L processing of CYC1 requires the covalent addition of a heme moiety to CYC1, catalyzed by holocytochrome c-type synthase (HCCS).
source: IMMP2L processing requires the covalent addition of a heme moiety to CYC1, catalyzed by holocytochrome c-type synthase (HCCS), and completes the formation of mature holo-CYC1 (Ndi et al., 2018; Nicholson et al., 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CYC1 levels were significantly reduced in OCIAD1 knockdown cells.
source: CYC1 levels were significantly reduced in OCIAD1 knockdown cells (Figure 5D and E), consistent with our unbiased mass spectrometry data (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Two larger molecular weight CYC1 species, likely corresponding to the precursor and intermediate forms, accumulated in OCIAD1 knockdown cells.
source: In addition, two larger molecular weight CYC1 species, likely corresponding to the precursor and intermediate forms, accumulated in OCIAD1 knockdown cells as compared to control cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: OCIAD1 function is required for normal CYC1 processing.
source: These data indicate that OCIAD1 function is required for normal CYC1 processing.
evidence: This is inferred from the accumulation of unprocessed CYC1 forms in OCIAD1 knockdown cells.

claim: The slower migrating CYC1 species that accumulate in OCIAD1 knockdown cells were fully hemylated.
source: The slower migrating CYC1 species that accumulate in OCIAD1 knockdown cells and OCIAD1 Δ97–115 truncated cells were fully hemylated (Figure 5D,E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on heme detection assays shown in Figure 5D, E, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: OCIAD1 knockdown cells have a CYC1 hemylation ratio comparable to mature CYC1 in control cells.
source: The hemylation levels of the slower-migrating CYC1 species in OCIAD1 knockdown cells were proportional to CYC1 abundance, indicating that OCIAD1 knockdown cells have a CYC1 hemylation ratio comparable to mature CYC1 in control cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on quantification of heme and CYC1 levels shown in Figure 5E.

claim: OCIAD1 is not required for CYC1 hemylation.
source: These data indicate that OCIAD1 is not required for CYC1 hemylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that unprocessed CYC1 in OCIAD1 knockdown cells is fully hemylated.

claim: The CYC1 maturation defect was not detected in OCIAD2 knockdown cells and was specific to loss of OCIAD1 function.
source: The CYC1 maturation defect was not detected in OCIAD2 knockdown cells and, thus, was specific to loss of OCIAD1 function (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: The processing of GPD2 and AIF, two additional substrates of IMMP2L, was unaffected in OCIAD1 knockdown cells.
source: The processing of GPD2 and AIF, two additional substrates of IMMP2L (Lu et al., 2008; Yuan et al., 2018), was unaffected in OCIAD1 knockdown cells as assessed by immunoblotting, suggesting that the maturation defect is specific to CYC1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: The maturation defect in OCIAD1 knockdown cells is specific to CYC1.
source: The processing of GPD2 and AIF, two additional substrates of IMMP2L (Lu et al., 2008; Yuan et al., 2018), was unaffected in OCIAD1 knockdown cells as assessed by immunoblotting, suggesting that the maturation defect is specific to CYC1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is inferred from the selective effect on CYC1 processing but not on other IMMP2L substrates.

claim: The extent of hemylation in CIII2 from OCIAD1 knockdown cells was comparable to that of wildtype cells.
source: Although CIII2 levels were reduced in OCIAD1 knockdown cells, the extent of hemylation in CIII2 was comparable to that of wildtype cells (compare Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on heme detection assays shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CIII2 from OCIAD1 knockdown cells contains higher molecular weight CYC1 species.
source: We also used 2D-native/SDS-PAGE and found that CIII2 from OCIAD1 knockdown cells contains higher molecular weight CYC1 species (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on 2D-native/SDS-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Unprocessed but hemylated CYC1 is incorporated in CIII2 in OCIAD1 knockdown cells.
source: Thus, unprocessed but hemylated CYC1 is incorporated in CIII2 in OCIAD1 knockdown cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of higher molecular weight hemylated CYC1 species in CIII2 from OCIAD1 knockdown cells.

claim: A peptide N-terminal to the CYC1 hydrophobic bipartite sequence was uniquely detected in CIII2 assemblies isolated from OCIAD1 knockdown cells.
source: We also identified a peptide (TPQAVALSSK), N-terminal to the CYC1 hydrophobic bipartite sequence, that was uniquely detected in CIII2 assemblies isolated from OCIAD1 knockdown cells (Figure 6B, lower panel), consistent with the accumulation of the precursor form of CYC1 in OCIAD1 knockdown cells.
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry analysis of BN-PAGE gel slices shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A peptide representing the N-terminus of mature CYC1 was only reliably identified in CIII2 assemblies from control and rescued cells, but not from OCIAD1 knockdown cells.
source: Conversely, a peptide (SDLELHPPSYPWSHR) representing the N-terminus of mature CYC1, as determined by N-terminome sequencing analysis of the human mitochondrial proteome (Vaca Jacome et al., 2015), was only reliably identified in CIII2 assemblies from control and rescued cells, but not from OCIAD1 knockdown cells (Figure 6B, middle panel).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry analysis of BN-PAGE gel slices shown in Figure 6B.

claim: OCIAD1 regulates the proteolytic processing and maturation of the holo-CYC1 precursor.
source: Taken together, our results are consistent with OCIAD1 regulating the proteolytic processing and maturation of the holo-CYC1 precursor.
evidence: This is inferred from the accumulation of unprocessed CYC1 forms and the peptide mapping data.

claim: Cytochrome bc1 complexes are highly conserved, found in photosynthetic and respiring bacterial plasma membranes of phylogenetically distant species, as well as in eukaryotic cells in mitochondria and in chloroplasts as the related cytochrome b6f complex.
source: Cytochrome bc1 complexes are highly conserved, found in photosynthetic and respiring bacterial plasma membranes of phylogenetically distant species, as well as in eukaryotic cells in mitochondria and in chloroplasts as the related cytochrome b6f complex (Trumpower, 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Cytochrome bc1 complexes in plants, fungi, and mammals exist as dimers (CIII2) displaying exceptional structural conservation of all three catalytic subunits despite modest sequence homology.
source: The comparison of high-resolution atomic models of cytochrome bc1 complexes in plants, fungi, and mammals revealed that despite their modest sequence homology, they exist as dimers (CIII2) displaying exceptional structural conservation of all three catalytic subunits (Maldonado et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In all CIII2 atomic models, mature holo-CYC1 possesses one C-terminal transmembrane helix and an N-terminal domain composed of six α-helices and two-strand β-sheet extending in the IMS.
source: In all CIII2 atomic models, mature holo-CYC1 possesses one C-terminal transmembrane helix and an N-terminal domain composed of six α-helices and two-strand β-sheet extending in the IMS (Maldonado et al., 2021; Xia et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The MTS of CYC1 is required for its targeting to mitochondria.
source: The MTS of CYC1 is required for its targeting to mitochondria; however, its removal by MPP is not required for the heme-dependent maturation of CYC1 by IMMP2L.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CYC1 import and processing.

claim: The removal of the MTS by MPP is not required for the heme-dependent maturation of CYC1 by IMMP2L.
source: The MTS of CYC1 is required for its targeting to mitochondria; however, its removal by MPP is not required for the heme-dependent maturation of CYC1 by IMMP2L.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CYC1 processing.

claim: Both precursor and intermediate forms of CYC1 can be hemylated and the bipartite sequence can be cleaved in a single step by the IMMP2L, without the removal of the MTS by the MPP.
source: Thus, both precursor and intermediate forms of CYC1 can be hemylated and the bipartite sequence can be cleaved in a single step by the IMMP2L, without the removal of the MTS by the MPP (Nicholson et al., 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Two fully hemylated CYC1 species of higher molecular weight that accumulate in OCIAD1 knockdown and mutant cells likely represent the precursor and intermediate holo-CYC1.
source: Consistent with this, two fully hemylated CYC1 species of higher molecular weight accumulate in OCIAD1 knockdown and mutant cells and likely represent the precursor and intermediate holo-CYC1.
evidence: This is inferred from the molecular weights and hemylation status of the accumulated CYC1 species.

claim: OCIAD1 regulates CYC1 processing by both MPP and IMMP2L.
source: Thus, overall, our results suggest that OCIAD1 regulates CYC1 processing by both MPP and IMMP2L.
evidence: This is inferred from the accumulation of both precursor and intermediate forms of CYC1 in OCIAD1 knockdown cells.

claim: OCIAD1 and its related paralog OCIAD2 are highly conserved in metazoans.
source: OCIAD1 and its related paralog OCIAD2 are highly conserved in metazoans.
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation analysis.

claim: Yil077c (Rci37), a yeast protein shown to interact with the CIII–CIV supercomplex, m-AAA proteases, and the prohibitin complex, was identified as a putative remote homolog of both OCIAD paralogs.
source: Yil077c (Rci37), a yeast protein shown to interact with the CIII–CIV supercomplex, m-AAA proteases, and the prohibitin complex (Morgenstern et al., 2017), was identified as a putative remote homolog of both OCIAD paralogs.
evidence: This is based on remote protein homology detection using HHpred analysis.

claim: The yeast protein COX20 was identified as a highly probable homolog of OCIAD1, but not OCIAD2.
source: The yeast protein COX20 was also identified as a highly probable homolog of OCIAD1, but not OCIAD2, and has a similar size and topology to OCIAD1.
evidence: This is based on remote protein homology detection using HHpred analysis.

claim: COX20 has a similar size and topology to OCIAD1.
source: The yeast protein COX20 was also identified as a highly probable homolog of OCIAD1, but not OCIAD2, and has a similar size and topology to OCIAD1.
evidence: This is based on comparison of protein properties.

claim: Both COX20 and OCIAD1 are integral inner membrane proteins with N- and C-termini located in the IMS.
source: Both proteins are integral inner membrane proteins with N- and C-termini located in the IMS (Tzagoloff et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: COX20 is a chaperone involved in the biogenesis of CIV, where it binds to newly synthesized mitochondrially encoded Cox2 and presents it to the inner membrane peptidase complex to facilitate the proteolytic removal of its N-terminal presequence by Imp2.
source: COX20 is a chaperone involved in the biogenesis of CIV, where it binds to newly synthesized mitochondrially encoded Cox2 and presents it to the inner membrane peptidase complex to facilitate the proteolytic removal of its N-terminal presequence by Imp2 (Elliott et al., 2012; Nunnari et al., 1993; Tzagoloff et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The high homology between COX20 and OCIAD1, but not OCIAD2, is consistent with the functional specialization of OCIAD paralogs.
source: The high homology between COX20 and OCIAD1, but not OCIAD2, is consistent with the functional specialization of OCIAD paralogs and suggests that OCIAD1 serves a conserved function in facilitating the proteolytic processing of CYC1.
evidence: This is inferred from the homology analysis and functional data.

claim: OCIAD1 serves a conserved function in facilitating the proteolytic processing of CYC1.
source: The high homology between COX20 and OCIAD1, but not OCIAD2, is consistent with the functional specialization of OCIAD paralogs and suggests that OCIAD1 serves a conserved function in facilitating the proteolytic processing of CYC1.
evidence: This is inferred from the homology to COX20 and the experimental data on CYC1 processing.

claim: Processing of CYC1 to its mature form is not essential for its function in CIII2 as mitochondrial respiration, including CIII2 activity, is not affected in IMMP2L mutant mice.
source: Processing of CYC1 to its mature form is not essential for its function in CIII2 as mitochondrial respiration, including CIII2 activity, is not affected in IMMP2L mutant mice (Bharadwaj et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Immature holo-CYC1 can be successfully incorporated into CIII2 and CIII2-containing supercomplexes in OCIAD1 knockdown and mutant cells.
source: Consistent with this, we found that immature holo-CYC1 can be successfully incorporated into CIII2 and CIII2-containing supercomplexes in OCIAD1 knockdown and mutant cells.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing hemylated unprocessed CYC1 in CIII2.

claim: CIII2 complexes containing immature holo-CYC1 may have increased superoxide production, which can be detrimental to mitochondrial function.
source: It is possible that CIII2 complexes containing immature holo-CYC1 have increased superoxide production, which can be detrimental to mitochondrial function (Lu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation.

claim: In contrast to IMMP2L mutant mice, steady-state levels of CYC1 were substantially reduced in OCIAD1 knockdown cells.
source: However, in contrast to IMMP2L mutant mice (Bharadwaj et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2008), steady-state levels of CYC1 were also substantially reduced in OCIAD1 knockdown cells, consistent with the observed antimycin A sensitization growth phenotype of OCIAD1 knockdown cells.
evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing OCIAD1 knockdown to IMMP2L mutant mice.

claim: OCIAD1 may also function as a chaperone that stabilizes newly imported CYC1.
source: This observation suggests that OCIAD1 may also function as a chaperone that stabilizes newly imported CYC1.
evidence: This is a speculative statement inferred from the reduced CYC1 levels in OCIAD1 knockdown cells.

claim: Under native conditions, a majority of OCIAD1 associates with prohibitins to form supramolecular complexes of ~1 MDa.
source: We demonstrate that under native conditions, a majority of OCIAD1 associates with prohibitins to form supramolecular complexes of ~1 MDa, consistent with published prohibitin interactomes (Richter-Dennerlein et al., 2014; Yoshinaka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on BN-PAGE analysis and supported by citations.

claim: OCIAD1 is likely a direct prohibitin interactor given that residue-to-residue contacts were identified between prohibitin and OCIAD1 peptides using cross-linking mass spectrometry analysis.
source: OCIAD1 is likely a direct prohibitin interactor given that residue-to-residue contacts were identified between prohibitin and OCIAD1 peptides using cross-linking mass spectrometry analysis (Liu et al., 2018; Yoshinaka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Prohibitins are members of the SPFH superfamily of scaffold proteins and form large ring-like structures in membranes, which are thought to create functionally specialized protein and lipid domains within the crowded environment of the IMM.
source: Prohibitins are members of the SPFH superfamily of scaffold proteins and form large ring-like structures in membranes, which are thought to create functionally specialized protein and lipid domains within the crowded environment of the IMM (Osman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Prohibitins and the related SPFH scaffold, SLP2, have been shown to sequester inner membrane associated proteases to gate their access to proteolytic substrates.
source: Consistent with this model, prohibitins and the related SPFH scaffold, SLP2, have been shown to sequester inner membrane associated proteases to gate their access to proteolytic substrates (Merkwirth et al., 2008; Steglich et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: IMMP2L was identified in the prohibitin interactome by proximity labeling.
source: IMMP2L was identified in the prohibitin interactome by proximity labeling (Yoshinaka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Within prohibitin assemblies, OCIAD1 targets precursor CYC1 to the IMMP2L peptidase.
source: Thus, we propose that within prohibitin assemblies, OCIAD1 targets precursor CYC1 to the IMMP2L peptidase.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.
